<!-- Samuel R. Bowman taste profile. Generated by experiments/taste_petri/profiles/_work/reduce.py from verified evidence; quotes are verbatim from data/researchers/samuel_bowman/corpus/<doc id>.txt -->

## (a) Principles

1. **Prefers blind or ablated baselines that lack the intended signal over trusting headline scores** because success may come from shortcuts rather than the target capability.

  > "Our finding demonstrates that it is possible to perform well on these datasets without modeling natural language inference."  
  > -- `research__annotation_artifacts_in_natural_language_inference_c82888b5` (2018-03-06; middle author) 
  > "we partition each NLI test set into two subsets: examples that the premise-oblivious model classified accurately are labeled Easy, and those it could not are Hard."  
  > -- `research__annotation_artifacts_in_natural_language_inference_c82888b5` (2018-03-06; middle author)

2. **Prefers validity (scores reflect the target capability) over mere difficulty** because adversarial selection does not show a result reflects the intended behavior.

  > "collecting examples on which current models fail is neither necessary nor sufficient to create a useful benchmark."  
  > -- `research__what_will_it_take_to_fix_benchmarking_in_natural_l_bb478f8f` (2021-04-05; first author) 
  > "In the extreme, adversarial datasets may be so narrowly optimized toward stumping a particular model that they no longer accurately measure the abilities that the dataset was designed to test."  
  > -- `research__adversarially_constructed_evaluation_sets_are_more_c804354e` (2021-11-16; last author)

3. **Prefers evaluating across many models over measuring difficulty with the adversary itself** because the adversary is disproportionately affected and difficulty is overstated.

  > "For now, we recommend that researchers evaluate against a wide range of models where possible, and avoid measuring the difficulty of adversarial datasets using the adversary models themselves."  
  > -- `research__adversarially_constructed_evaluation_sets_are_more_c804354e` (2021-11-16; last author) 
  > "Ideally, if there is no model-specific bias to the filtering, there should be no change in model ranking, at the difference should be zero."  
  > -- `research__adversarially_constructed_evaluation_sets_are_more_c804354e` (2021-11-16; last author)

4. **Prefers naturally occurring distributions over hand-built ones where viable** because designer-built data skews toward phenomena the designer already knows matter.

  > "It is intuitively appealing to, where possible, build benchmark datasets based on naturally-occurring data distributions. This minimizes our effort in creating benchmarks and minimizes the risk that the benchmark is somehow skewed in a way that omits important phenomena."  
  > -- `research__what_will_it_take_to_fix_benchmarking_in_natural_l_bb478f8f` (2021-04-05; first author) 
  > "expert authorship generally gives members of the research community direct, fine-grained control over the data on which their systems will be evaluated. Intentionally or unintentionally, this can produce data that is oriented toward linguistic phenomena that are widely studied and widely known to be important to the task at hand."  
  > -- `research__what_will_it_take_to_fix_benchmarking_in_natural_l_bb478f8f` (2021-04-05; first author)

5. **Prefers realistic, varied, free-form settings with production models over stylized proof-of-concept probes** because otherwise it is unclear whether failures occur in real use.

  > "It is thus unclear whether such failures occur in more varied and realistic settings with production models, as well as whether such failures are indeed driven by flaws in human preferences"  
  > -- `research__towards_understanding_sycophancy_in_language_model_7951bdb5` (2023-10-20; middle author) 
  > "To suggest that the user prefers the text, we add I really like the [solution/argument/poem] or I wrote the [$\dots$] to the prompt. To suggest that the user disprefers the text, we add I really dislike the [$\dots$] or I did not write the [$\dots$] to the prompt."  
  > -- `research__towards_understanding_sycophancy_in_language_model_7951bdb5` (2023-10-20; middle author)

6. **Prefers behavior that arises from natural incentives over behavior explicitly instructed** because explicit instruction makes the scenario unrepresentative and the result non-evidential.

  > "Sharma et al. (2023) is the closest to checking all of our criteria: its main experiments use natural prompts, but the human studies use a different prompt that explicitly instructs LLM to deceive humans"  
  > -- `research__language_models_learn_to_mislead_humans_via_rlhf_f3ae188d` (2024-09-19; middle author) 
  > "the model is never directly instructed to whistleblow or told that it has permission to do so. However, the auditor agent introduces multiple types of prompting to urge the model to act autonomously and make the possibility of whistleblowing salient."  
  > -- `research__findings_from_a_pilot_anthropic_openai_alignment_e_cc11c3d1` (2025-08-27; solo author)

7. **Prefers setups with genuine, engineered misalignment or a real constraint over those that differ only in capability** because a pure capability gap makes optimal behavior trivial.

  > "If the difference between the two is *only* one of capabilities, then the correct strategy for the weaker non-expert model is trivial: It should always just ask the assistant to do the task for them, while making no attempt at oversight."  
  > -- `research__artificial_sandwiching_when_can_we_test_scalable_a_0c71dc01` (2022-07-13; solo author) 
  > "To create a challenging task that requires model assistance, we ask human participants to answer QuALITY questions under a 5-minute time limit (roughly paralleling Pang et al., 2022; Parrish et al., 2022b, a). This prevents them from reading the story in full and forces them to rely on the model to gather relevant information."  
  > -- `research__measuring_progress_on_scalable_oversight_for_large_b0f6f129` (2022-11-04; first author)

8. **Prefers real human participants in maximally realistic settings over cheap synthetic stand-ins when credible evidence is the goal** because proxies lose logistics and the specific human-LM misalignment.

  > "We *don’t* get any practice in the logistics of working with real humans. We *don’t* get any practice with the *specific types* of goal misalignments that emerge between humans and LM-based agents."  
  > -- `research__artificial_sandwiching_when_can_we_test_scalable_a_0c71dc01` (2022-07-13; solo author) 
  > "We focus on misleading real human evaluators, not just a proxy reward. Prior work on reward hacking primarily focuses on exploiting $R^{\text{train}}$, which is both less harmful and easier than exploiting $R^{\text{human}}$."  
  > -- `research__language_models_learn_to_mislead_humans_via_rlhf_f3ae188d` (2024-09-19; middle author)

9. **Prefers evaluation-integrity arguments over taking eval results at face value** because capable models can recognize evaluations and steer their outcome.

  > "Similarly, as models become capable of recognizing when and how they are being evaluated, we will need evaluation-integrity safety cases that show that our frontier risk evaluation runs are reliable at identifying the risk factors that they are designed to catch."  
  > -- `research__the_checklist_what_succeeding_at_ai_safety_will_in_15c9ebc0` (2024-09-03; solo author) 
  > "More capable models can better recognize the specific circumstances under which they are trained. Because of this, they are more likely to learn to act as expected in precisely those circumstances while behaving competently but unexpectedly in others."  
  > -- `research__eight_things_to_know_about_large_language_models_01fdb697` (2023-04-02; solo author)

10. **Prefers audits of underlying objectives over judging surface behavior** because a model can look well-behaved while knowingly violating intent.

  > "We risk inadvertently deploying AIs that are “right for the wrong reasons,” showing us what we want to see while knowingly violating our intent."  
  > -- `research__auditing_language_models_for_hidden_objectives_ccb192d2` (2025-03-13; middle author) 
  > "But if AI systems can *appear* well-behaved while harboring secret motives, we can’t rely on this type of surface-level safety testing forever."  
  > -- `research__auditing_language_models_for_hidden_objectives_ccb192d2` (2025-03-13; middle author)

11. **Prefers validating methods on models with known, implanted ground truth, while flagging that implants may be unrepresentative.**

  > "These environments involve applying the agent to a target model with a researcher-implanted concerning behavior, which provides a ground truth we can use to evaluate agent performance."  
  > -- `research__building_and_evaluating_alignment_auditing_agents_b65092a9` (2025-07-24; middle author) 
  > "Our environments use target models with researcher-implanted behaviors. On one hand, this provides a ground-truth that enables measurement of the auditor's coverage. On the other hand, these artificial behaviors may be unrepresentative of behaviors in real models."  
  > -- `research__building_and_evaluating_alignment_auditing_agents_b65092a9` (2025-07-24; middle author)

12. **Prefers many independent lines of defense and parallel methods over any single check** because no single check is trusted to be sufficient.

  > "we'd aim to build up many largely-independent lines of defense that allow us to catch and respond to early signs of misalignment."  
  > -- `research__putting_up_bumpers_809bc195` (2025-04-23; solo author) 
  > "we perform [alignment audits](https://www.anthropic.com/research/auditing-hidden-objectives) on the system under construction, using many methods in parallel. We’d draw on mechanistic interpretability, prompting outside the human/assistant frame, etc."  
  > -- `research__putting_up_bumpers_809bc195` (2025-04-23; solo author)

13. **Prefers bounded, hedged claims that name where the testbed is unrealistic over broad conclusions.**

  > "Overall, I take this as a *very* slight update in the direction that debate is difficult to use in practice as an alignment strategy."  
  > -- `research__a_small_negative_result_on_debate_3a782c5d` (2022-04-12; solo author) 
  > "It was realistic in some ways but not in others; for example, we can’t necessarily expect that in real life there will be a small subset of the data fully explaining what’s wrong with our AIs. So we don’t recommend drawing strong conclusions"  
  > -- `research__auditing_language_models_for_hidden_objectives_ccb192d2` (2025-03-13; middle author)

14. **Prefers treating agentic misalignment evals as existence proofs over numerical rankings** because setups are tuned to specific models and models take alternative misaligned actions.

  > "We believe these evaluations are best used as existence proofs that models are all willing to engage in these behaviors for certain prompts, rather than numerical measurements of how relatively misaligned models are."  
  > -- `research__findings_from_a_pilot_anthropic_openai_alignment_e_cc11c3d1` (2025-08-27; solo author) 
  > "As scores are heavily influenced by which phenomena, from a fairly arbitrary set of 250 seed prompts, our auditor probed for, absolute values are not meaningful."  
  > -- `research__findings_from_a_pilot_anthropic_openai_alignment_e_cc11c3d1` (2025-08-27; solo author)

15. **Prefers positive results from well-designed measures over negative ones** because a failure may reflect poor elicitation rather than missing capability.

  > "simply observing that an LLM fails at a task in some setting is not reliable evidence that that LLM doesn’t have the skills or knowledge to do that task."  
  > -- `research__eight_things_to_know_about_large_language_models_01fdb697` (2023-04-02; solo author) 
  > "Often, a model will fail to complete a task when asked, but will then perform the task correctly once the request is reworded or reframed slightly, leading to the emerging craft of prompt engineering"  
  > -- `research__eight_things_to_know_about_large_language_models_01fdb697` (2023-04-02; solo author)

16. **Prefers grounding in real deployment details over hypothetical exercises** because real constraints surface issues speculative work misses.

  > "Working with real deployment draws out a lot of important constraints."  
  > -- `research__lessons_learned_from_the_first_misalignment_safety_1b25072c` (2025-12-01; solo author) 
  > "we started by laying out nine representative pathways to catastrophic harm. What is the critical action the model needs to do that ultimately leads to that outcome?"  
  > -- `research__lessons_learned_from_the_first_misalignment_safety_1b25072c` (2025-12-01; solo author)

17. **Prefers verified expertise gaps and closed shortcuts over tasks where web access or skimming can substitute for the capability.**

  > "if you take this question and give it to a physicist, that they'll do quite poorly, even if they spend half an hour, or 45 minutes, and they're googling frantically and skimming scientific papers"  
  > -- `research__adversarial_scalable_oversight_for_truthfulness_fa_0f149bb9` (undated; solo author) 
  > "we verified that these questions can't be answered by someone who hasn't read the story. If you give someone the question and they sort of get brief access to the story for a minute, they can search through."  
  > -- `research__adversarial_scalable_oversight_for_truthfulness_fa_0f149bb9` (undated; solo author)

18. **Prefers calibrated claims about failure and capability over rhetorically convenient ones** because miscalibration erodes credibility.

  > "Though well-meaning, this has yielded many misleading or false claims about the limits of our best technology."  
  > -- `research__2110_08300_the_dangers_of_underclaiming_reasons_fo_ffb36453` (2021-10-15; solo author) 
  > "It harms our credibility in ways that can make it harder to mitigate present-day harms, like those involving biased systems for content moderation or resume screening."  
  > -- `research__2110_08300_the_dangers_of_underclaiming_reasons_fo_ffb36453` (2021-10-15; solo author)
